A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.
Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.
Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn.
The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure company Axiom Solutions International , TypeSafe AI a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI .
Familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch.
New unicorns in October 2026
Here are October’s new unicorn companies by industry segment.
AI models, assistants and agents
TypeSafe AI : San Francisco-based AI model developer TypeSafe AI raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with participation from DCVC and Sequoia Capital. The 2-year-old company develops an AI model Jev for structured decision-making, helping applications automate tasks such as classification, scoring and routing with confidence estimates.
Manus AI : Singapore-based AI assistant Manus AI raised $500 million at a $4 billion valuation. Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the round. The 3-year-old company develops general-purpose AI agents that perform tasks including research, browser automation, content creation and software development. Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025, but Chinese regulators intervened and ordered the transaction reversed.
Nous Research : Austin-based Nous Research, developer of the Hermes agent, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the financing, with investors including Nvidia , Microsoft’s M12 , Menlo Ventures and Union Square Ventures . The 3-year-old company develops open-source AI models, agents and infrastructure for AI development and deployment. Nous Research built the open-source Hermes Agent, which it is deploying for businesses.
Upstage : South Korea-based Upstage, developer of the open-source Solar model, raised $30 million in Series C funding, reaching $1.5 billion in value. The 6-year-old company develops the Solar language models and document-processing technology that converts unstructured business information into usable data for the future of work.
Wabi : San Francisco-based personal AI assistant Wabi raised a $55 million Series A at a $1.25 billion valuation. IVP led the financing, joined by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Forerunner and Amazon’s Alexa Fund . The 1-year-old company develops an AI personal assistant for everyday activities such as planning trips, coordinating meals and organizing tasks.
Town : San Francisco-based Town, a developer of a workforce AI assistant, raised a $108 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. Forerunner and Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, First Round Capital and other investors. The 2-year-old company develops personalized AI assistants that connect with workplace tools across teams to manage email, prepare meeting briefings, organize schedules and complete recurring tasks.
Aerospace, defense and space
Air Space Intelligence : Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which makes AI software for national security, raised a $325 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Spark Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Citadel Securities , Craft Ventures , Energy Impact Partners and Meritech Capital Partners . The 8-year-old company develops AI software for managing complex physical operations across aviation, defense, energy and logistics.
Xona : Burlingame, California-based Xona, which says it’s developing a better satellite navigation system, raised a $250 million Series D at a $2.45 billion valuation. Future Ventures led the round, with participation from Industrious Ventures and Woven Capital . candidates.title: Anthropic Seeks Record $88.5B Tied To Public Market Debut
candidates.snippet: Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut. Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.
On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.
Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut.
An IPO and a private placement
The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.
For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.
Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC .
Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
Revenue and recent updates
Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.
For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.
The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.
As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

candidates.title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
candidates.snippet: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.

Gené Teare

More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.
The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.
Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)
That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.
The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.
At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.
“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.
This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.
Go big and early — or wait
Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.
With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.
Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”
Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.
The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.
“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”
Deals sizes trend higher
At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.
Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.
Raising a large Series A
For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.
“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures , whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.
“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.
She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.
But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

Ferguson: $9 Billion In Third-Quarter Sales, 9.5% Growth, And Raised 2026 Guidance
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 3:07 AM
Ferguson: $9 Billion In Third-Quarter Sales, 9.5% Growth, And Raised 2026 Guidance
Ferguson Enterprises, a North American distributor of water and air solutions, reported third-quarter 2026 sales of $9.03 billion, representing a 9.5% increase from the prior year, supported by organic growth, acquisitions, and strong demand across non-residential markets. The company also raised its full-year sales growth outlook following continued operating momentum and the acquisition of FloWorks.
For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, Ferguson generated organic sales growth of 7%, while acquisitions contributed an additional 2.7 percentage points. The company reported operating profit of $885 million, up 4.9% year over year, and adjusted operating profit of $962 million, an increase of 8.9%.
Gross margin declined 40 basis points to 30.9%, while reported operating margin decreased to 9.8% from 10.2% a year earlier. Adjusted operating margin remained unchanged at 10.7%.
Reported diluted earnings per share declined 4.9% to $3.08, compared with $3.24 in the prior-year quarter. However, adjusted diluted earnings per share increased 7.9% to $3.43, reflecting higher adjusted operating profit.
Ferguson’s U.S. business continued to drive growth, with sales increasing 10.2% year over year. Non-residential sales rose 15%, supported by large capital projects, healthy bidding activity, and demand for specialized solutions. Residential sales increased 6% despite continued weakness in new construction and repair, maintenance, and improvement activity.
The Canadian business experienced more challenging conditions, with sales declining 4.5%, reflecting divestments and unfavorable foreign exchange movements.
Acquisitions remained a central component of Ferguson’s expansion strategy. The company completed three acquisitions during the quarter, including FloWorks, Brax Company, and Rogers Supply Company. Following the quarter, Ferguson also acquired Canyon Systems, expanding its water and wastewater treatment capabilities.
Ferguson has completed 11 acquisitions during 2026, representing approximately $1.5 billion in aggregate annualized revenue. The company invested $1.7 billion in acquisitions during the third quarter, including FloWorks, while deploying $108 million in capital expenditures.
Following the FloWorks acquisition, Ferguson reported net debt to adjusted EBITDA of 1.7 times, compared with 1.0 times a year earlier.
For the first nine months of 2026, Ferguson generated $25.25 billion in sales, an increase of 6%, while adjusted operating profit increased 6.5% to $2.54 billion. Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.73 billion, up 6.9%.
Based on its year-to-date performance and the contribution from FloWorks, Ferguson increased its calendar 2026 sales growth guidance from mid-single-digit growth to approximately 7%. The company also raised the lower end of its adjusted operating margin outlook, establishing a revised range of 9.6% to 9.8%, compared with the previous range of 9.5% to 9.8%.
The updated outlook includes approximately $235 million in interest expense and $425 million in capital expenditures.
Ferguson also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.89 per share, payable January 8, 2027, to shareholders of record as of November 20, 2026.
KEY QUOTES:
“Our expert associates delivered strong third quarter results, with non-residential sales up 15% and residential growth of 6%. We continue to invest organically and through acquisitions to expand our value-added solutions and geographic footprint. We have completed eleven acquisitions this year with an aggregate annualized revenue of approximately $1.5 billion, while preserving a strong balance sheet.
“While our markets remain mixed, our year-to-date performance and the addition of FloWorks enable us to raise our full year guidance. We expect to continue delivering market outperformance by deploying scale locally and leveraging the long-term growth drivers of water infrastructure, large capital projects, climate and comfort and aging and underbuilt housing. We remain confident in our ability to capitalize on these growth drivers as we provide essential water and air solutions for the complex project needs of the specialized professional.”
Kevin Murphy, Chief Executive Officer, Ferguson

candidates.text:
Surgery Partners: HealthSpan Partners Raises Merger Offer To $25 Per Share In Deal Valued At Up To $6 Billion
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 3:32 PM
Surgery Partners: HealthSpan Partners Raises Merger Offer To $25 Per Share In Deal Valued At Up To $6 Billion
Surgery Partners and HealthSpan Partners have amended their merger agreement to increase the cash consideration for Surgery Partners shareholders to $25 per share, with the total enterprise value potentially reaching approximately $6 billion. The revised agreement follows an unsolicited competing acquisition proposal and includes additional payments for certain shareholders if the transaction closes after March 1, 2027.
HealthSpan Partners is affiliated with Bon Secours Mercy Health and is pursuing the acquisition of Surgery Partners, an operator of outpatient surgical facilities across the United States.
The amendment represents an increase in the merger consideration and introduces a mechanism to compensate eligible shareholders for certain closing delays.
Under the amended agreement, shareholders other than affiliates of Bain Capital will receive $25 per share in cash if the transaction closes before March 1, 2027.
If the required shareholder approval has been obtained but the transaction remains incomplete after that date, eligible shareholders will receive additional monthly payments.
These payments will accrue at a rate equivalent to 10% annually on the $25-per-share merger consideration.
If the transaction closes on its October 23, 2027 outside date and the applicable conditions are satisfied, those payments could total up to $1.61 per share.
That would increase the maximum consideration for eligible shareholders to $26.61 per share.
The revised merger agreement follows an unsolicited, nonbinding competing proposal received on November 3, 2026, and updated on November 8.
The competing bidder offered $28 per share in cash to acquire all outstanding Surgery Partners shares.
Although the competing proposal offered a higher stated price, Surgery Partners’ independent special committee considered additional factors involving transaction certainty and closing timing.
The committee evaluated the likelihood that the competing transaction would receive regulatory approvals and the potential consequences of a longer completion process.
It also considered the contractual protections available under each proposal.
Following consultation with legal and financial advisors, the special committee unanimously determined that the competing offer did not constitute a superior proposal under the existing merger agreement.
The committee recommended that Surgery Partners proceed with the amended HealthSpan transaction.
The company’s Board of Directors approved the revised agreement and reaffirmed its recommendation that shareholders vote in favor of the merger.
Bain Capital, which owns approximately 39% of Surgery Partners’ outstanding shares, has agreed to support the transaction.
Rather than receiving cash consideration, Bain Capital affiliates will exchange their Surgery Partners shares for ownership interests in the acquiring entity.
The arrangement will allow Bain Capital to remain a significant investor alongside HealthSpan Partners after closing.
Surgery Partners operates more than 200 locations across 30 states.
Its facilities include ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals, multispecialty physician practices, and urgent care locations.
The company focuses on providing surgical care through outpatient and other short-stay healthcare settings.
The combination with HealthSpan is intended to support expansion of outpatient care services through relationships with physicians and healthcare systems.
HealthSpan plans to finance the acquisition using cash on hand and new debt financing supported by existing commitments.
The merger is expected to close during the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder approval, regulatory clearances, and other closing conditions.
Centerview Partners is serving as lead financial advisor to Surgery Partners, while Leerink Partners is also providing financial advice.
Moelis & Company is advising the independent special committee.
Jefferies is serving as exclusive financial advisor to HealthSpan and has provided committed financing support.
The revised transaction reflects Surgery Partners’ decision to prioritize the combination of increased cash consideration, contractual protections, and expected closing certainty.
KEY QUOTE:
“We are pleased to have reached this outcome, which reflects the rigorous focus of our Board of Directors and Special Committee throughout this process on delivering the best possible result for Surgery Partners and our stockholders. This transaction provides exceptional value for our stockholders, along with regulatory certainty and a closing expected in the near term. We continue to believe combining with HealthSpan Partners is the right next chapter for our company as, together with our physician and health system partners, we expand access to high-quality outpatient care across the communities we serve.”
Eric Evans, CEO Of Surgery Partners

Mubadala Capital: LSV Advisors $5 Billion Secondaries Platform To Receive Strategic Minority Investment
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:38 AM
Mubadala Capital: LSV Advisors $5 Billion Secondaries Platform To Receive Strategic Minority Investment
Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset management subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Company, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire a minority ownership stake in LSV Advisors, a New York-based investment manager specializing in GP-led secondary transactions. The partnership will expand Mubadala Capital’s alternative investment capabilities while supporting the continued growth of LSV, which manages approximately $5 billion in assets and commitments.
Founded in 2005, LSV has established a specialized investment strategy focused on general partner-led continuation vehicles, particularly single-asset transactions involving middle-market companies.
The firm has completed more than 75 transactions since executing one of the industry’s earliest GP-led investments in 2011.
Continuation vehicles have become an increasingly important segment of the private equity secondary market, providing investment managers with an alternative to selling portfolio companies through traditional exit transactions.
These structures allow general partners to transfer investments from an existing fund into a new investment vehicle, often providing existing limited partners with an opportunity to receive liquidity or maintain exposure to the underlying business.
For fund managers, continuation vehicles can create additional time to execute growth strategies at portfolio companies while introducing new capital partners.
LSV focuses on identifying established, cash-generative businesses and structuring investments that emphasize governance, risk management, and alignment among stakeholders.
The company’s approach combines investment due diligence with transaction structures designed to address the interests of general partners, existing investors, and new capital providers.
The investment will add dedicated GP-led secondaries expertise to Mubadala Capital’s expanding portfolio of strategic partnerships.
Mubadala Capital currently maintains investment relationships across private wealth, insurance, credit, and real estate.
The LSV partnership will complement those activities by providing exposure to a specialized segment of the private equity market.

Constellation Energy: $1.8 Billion Q3 Net Income, Raised 2026 Guidance, And $5 Billion Nuclear Financing Commitment
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 3:01 AM
Constellation Energy: $1.8 Billion Q3 Net Income, Raised 2026 Guidance, And $5 Billion Nuclear Financing Commitment
Constellation Energy Corporation reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $1.835 billion, compared with $930 million a year earlier, as the company benefited from favorable market conditions and the addition of Calpine. The energy producer also raised the midpoint of its full-year adjusted operating earnings guidance while advancing major nuclear power agreements with Amazon and Google.
For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, Constellation reported GAAP earnings of $5.19 per share, compared with $2.97 in the prior-year period. Adjusted operating earnings increased to $1.792 billion, or $5.06 per share, from $952 million, or $3.04 per share, a year earlier.
The company narrowed its full-year adjusted operating earnings guidance to $12.50 to $12.80 per share, raising the midpoint for the second time in 2026.
Constellation attributed its quarterly performance primarily to favorable market and portfolio conditions and the addition of Calpine, which it acquired in January 2026. Higher interest costs and unfavorable nuclear production tax credit portfolio effects partially offset those benefits.
Beyond its financial results, Constellation highlighted several agreements intended to expand electricity generation capacity and support growing demand from technology companies and other large energy customers.
In September, Constellation announced a 20-year, 690-megawatt power purchase agreement with Amazon, along with a related retail supply agreement supporting Amazon’s operations in the PJM electricity market. The arrangement will enable more than $3 billion in infrastructure investments at the Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, including facility improvements and a 190-megawatt capacity expansion expected between 2030 and 2032.
In October, Constellation announced a separate 20-year power purchase agreement with Google supporting more than $4.3 billion in investments across 11 nuclear generating units in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey.
The Google agreement is expected to add approximately 890 megawatts of incremental nuclear generation capacity to the PJM grid, with the first uprate scheduled for 2028. Constellation also entered into a 15-year financial energy load-following agreement with Google covering 2,700 megawatts.
Together, the Amazon and Google arrangements support more than 1,000 megawatts of additional nuclear generating capacity.
Constellation also signed a conditional loan commitment with the U.S. Department of Energy for up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates. Subject to execution of a final loan agreement, the financing would involve a 30-year loan from the Federal Financing Bank, backed by a federal guarantee.
The company additionally agreed to acquire the Rhode Island State Energy Center from Shell Energy North America for $715 million, subject to customary adjustments and regulatory approvals. The 609-megawatt natural gas-fired facility operates in the ISO New England wholesale electricity market and would become part of Constellation’s merchant generation portfolio.
Another development was Constellation’s first Peak+ agreement, a 20-year arrangement covering 270 megawatts of energy, capacity, and nuclear attributes beginning in 2028. Peak+ combines additional generation and demand-response capabilities with energy products tailored to large customers.
Operationally, Constellation’s nuclear fleet generated 46,677 gigawatt-hours of electricity during the quarter, compared with 46,477 gigawatt-hours a year earlier. Excluding its Salem and South Texas Project interests, its nuclear facilities achieved a 97.2% capacity factor, up from 96.8% in the comparable period.
Constellation operates a diversified generation portfolio totaling approximately 55 gigawatts of capacity, spanning nuclear, natural gas, oil, geothermal, hydroelectric, wind, and solar facilities.
KEY QUOTES
“This past quarter Constellation announced agreements that are helping meet one of the nation’s greatest challenges – powering a growing economy while protecting existing customers. These agreements add more than 1,000 megawatts of new, emissions-free generation to the grid and help ensure the continued operations of existing clean power for generations to come. The new megawatts, which are the equivalent of a new large-scale nuclear plant, are coming online with no costs being borne by existing customers. We’re building on that progress with Peak+, an integrated solution that brings together new capacity, including new generation and demand response, with energy products to help large customers meet their evolving needs. Our approach proves we can power the growing digital economy while strengthening our electric grid – all with private investment.”
Joe Dominguez, Chairman, President And Chief Executive Officer, Constellation Energy
“Third quarter adjusted operating earnings were $5.06 per share, compared with $3.04 a year ago. This strong performance allowed us to raise the midpoint of our adjusted operating earnings guidance range for the second time this year. Our disciplined capital allocation strategy, including accretive organic growth through nuclear uprates, the acquisition of Rhode Island State Energy Center and our continued aggressive pace of share repurchases, positions us to deliver sustained earnings growth.”
Shane Smith, Executive Vice President And Chief Financial Officer, Constellation Energy

Eldridge: Stonebriar Closes $869 Million Equipment Asset-Backed Securitization
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 2:47 PM
Eldridge: Stonebriar Closes $869 Million Equipment Asset-Backed Securitization
Eldridge Capital Management has announced the closing of an $869 million equipment asset-backed securitization by Stonebriar Commercial Finance, an Eldridge-managed company. The financing, designated SCFET 2026-1, represents Stonebriar’s 16th equipment asset-backed securitization and expands the firm’s access to capital for financing essential business equipment across multiple industries.
Eldridge Diversified Credit Fund II also participated in the transaction, bringing together two components of Eldridge’s diversified credit platform.
The securitization is backed by leases and loans secured by essential-use assets across the marine, mining, energy, manufacturing, and technology sectors.
These financing arrangements support businesses that require substantial capital investments in specialized equipment and other income-producing assets.
Asset-backed securitizations allow lenders to package financial assets into securities purchased by institutional investors, creating an additional source of funding for their lending activities.
For Stonebriar, the approach has become an established component of its financing strategy.
The latest transaction builds on approximately $11 billion of asset-backed securities placed through the platform since 2016.
Stonebriar’s securitization program supports its ability to originate large equipment financing transactions while managing funding costs and maintaining access to capital markets.
The participation of Eldridge Diversified Credit Fund II represents an additional opportunity to connect the firm’s private credit investment activities with Stonebriar’s established financing infrastructure.
Eldridge believes the arrangement can provide benefits to its diversified credit strategy by leveraging the funding capabilities Stonebriar has developed over the past decade.
The securities issued through SCFET 2026-1 received ratings from Fitch Ratings and KBRA.
Bank of America served as sole structuring agent and lead bookrunner for the transaction.
BNP Paribas, Truist, and Wells Fargo participated as joint lead bookrunners.
The financing highlights continued institutional demand for securities backed by equipment loans and leases involving essential business assets.
Since 2015, the broader Eldridge platform has originated more than $19 billion in large-ticket equipment finance transactions on behalf of Stonebriar and Eldridge’s diversified credit funds.
The platform finances assets supporting activities such as manufacturing, transportation, electricity generation, chemicals, and other capital-intensive operations.
According to Monitor’s 2026 rankings cited by Eldridge, the firm operates North America’s largest private, independent equipment finance platform by both assets and origination volume.
Eldridge manages a broader portfolio of businesses and investments spanning asset management, infrastructure, insurance, defense and security, minerals, and media.
The latest securitization provides Stonebriar with additional funding capacity while demonstrating how Eldridge can coordinate its equipment finance and private credit activities.
As companies continue investing in essential industrial and technology infrastructure, the transaction reinforces Stonebriar’s position as a provider of financing for large, mission-critical assets.
KEY QUOTE:
“Bringing EDCF II into Stonebriar’s financing technology is an innovative step for us. The EDCF program gets the benefit of Stonebriar’s cost-effective funding, built over a decade, and we remain grateful to the funding partners who have supported us in placing almost $11 billion of ABS bonds since 2016.”
Nicholas Sandler, Co-President And Co-Head Of Diversified Credit At Eldridge Capital Management

Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 3:26 PM
Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion
Edgevana, an AI computing infrastructure company, has secured more than $700 million in fully committed, multiyear agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell computing systems across North America and Europe. The contracts expand the company’s committed customer demand to approximately $7 billion, with an additional active business pipeline exceeding $20 billion.
The agreements involve take-or-pay commitments under which customers contract for computing capacity over multiple years.
Edgevana intends to deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs and GB300 systems through its distributed data center infrastructure.
The company is developing a model that combines existing power availability, data center facilities, computing equipment, and high-speed network connectivity.
By coordinating these resources across multiple locations, Edgevana aims to accelerate the delivery of production-ready AI computing capacity.
The company says its approach can bring tens of megawatts of high-density AI infrastructure online within approximately 90 to 120 days.
Traditional data center development projects can require substantially longer timelines because of challenges involving land acquisition, utility connections, power infrastructure, equipment procurement, and construction.
Edgevana’s strategy centers on identifying locations where power and other essential infrastructure are already available.
The company then coordinates deployment of computing systems across its network, creating what it describes as a virtual campus.
This approach allows customers to access distributed infrastructure through a unified management environment.
Edgevana believes the model is particularly relevant as AI workloads shift from centralized model training toward inference applications supporting active users and business systems.
Inference workloads can require low latency, reliable network connectivity, and geographically distributed computing resources.
These requirements create opportunities for infrastructure providers capable of deploying AI compute closer to end users.
Edgevana’s experience includes providing low-latency infrastructure for high-frequency trading and supporting edge computing operations for two major hyperscale technology companies.
The company is applying those capabilities to the deployment of advanced AI accelerators.
Its global infrastructure network includes 17 operational data center locations, with another 10 sites under active development.
According to Edgevana, platforms supported by its infrastructure serve more than 10,000 downstream enterprise customers.
The company’s business model combines long-term energy supply arrangements, access to GPU computing equipment, and committed customer contracts.
By securing customer demand before deployment, Edgevana seeks to reduce financial exposure and improve capital efficiency.
The approach is also intended to help customers avoid delays associated with constructing entirely new data centers.
Edgevana believes pre-energized infrastructure can provide a competitive advantage as demand for high-performance AI computing increases.
Power availability has become an important constraint in the development of large AI data centers.
Companies seeking to deploy substantial computing capacity must secure reliable electricity supply while coordinating physical infrastructure and network requirements.
Edgevana’s platform is designed to address these challenges through coordinated deployment across multiple sites.
The latest $700 million in agreements will support deployment of next-generation NVIDIA computing systems in North America and Europe.
The company’s broader $7 billion in committed demand reflects customer contracts, while its more than $20 billion pipeline represents potential additional business rather than completed commitments.
Founded in 2019, Edgevana intends to continue expanding its network and accelerating deployment of AI infrastructure.
The company is positioning its distributed model as an alternative to relying exclusively on large, centralized data center campuses.
By combining available power, high-performance computing equipment, and network infrastructure, Edgevana aims to reduce deployment timelines and support customers requiring dedicated AI capacity.
KEY QUOTES:
“We stayed in stealth through the initial training boom on purpose, and in many ways, we still operate that way because our model isn’t obvious to the broader market. Training rewards centralized mega–campuses, but inference is live production traffic. As performance demands increase, it plays directly into our core strengths. We cut our teeth delivering ultra-low latency for high-frequency trading and managing edge production for two of the world’s largest hyperscalers. Now that AI is pivoting to inference, the market has come to us.”
Ryan Fay, Co-CEO Of Edgevana
“The defining constraint on AI isn’t algorithms or software, it’s physical, heavy-duty infrastructure. While the market focused exclusively on mega-gigawatt campuses, we spent years quietly securing the power, land, and compute required to bring infrastructure closer to the end user. African tech companies raised $684 million in the first nine months of 2026, according to a Tracxn Technologies report cited by AU-Startups, representing a 30% year-on-year increase from $527 million in the same period of 2025. The total was deployed across 100 funding rounds, slightly fewer than the 103 rounds recorded the year before.
The report found that Nairobi led African startup fundraising, attracting $277 million—about 41% of the continent-wide total for the period. The concentration is largely linked to a single transaction: Spiro’s $215 million Series E round in Nairobi, which followed the company’s broader $270 million funding round completed in June 2026.
Funding growth alongside fewer deals
While overall capital increased, the number of rounds fell by 3% year on year, signaling a more selective environment for investors. The report describes a trend in which capital is increasingly directed toward larger transactions and businesses demonstrating clear commercial potential, rather than earlier-stage ventures.
For early-stage founders—particularly those at pre-seed and seed—this environment can make fundraising more challenging, the report suggests, as investors focus on later-stage traction and scale-ready models.

The company operates across seven African countries, including Kenya, Rwanda and Nigeria. Table Of Contents
Apollo Global Management ( N7I.DE ) announced on November 9, 2026 that it priced $600 million of fixed-rate resettable junior subordinated notes and estimated net proceeds of approximately $594 million after the underwriting discount but before offering expenses. The notes carry a 7.550% initial coupon and mature on December 15, 2056.
The final pricing terms set the public price at 100.000% of principal, plus accrued interest, if any. Settlement is expected on November 13, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. Apollo intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including funding its previously announced investment in Mubadala Capital Asset Management, and to pay related fees and expenses. J.P. Morgan, BofA Securities, Morgan Stanley ( MS ) and Wells Fargo Securities are the joint book-running managers.
Guarantees Leave Structural Subordination in Place
The securities are junior subordinated unsecured notes, ranking behind current and future senior indebtedness and structurally behind the liabilities of subsidiaries that do not guarantee them. Six holding companies will fully and unconditionally guarantee the notes jointly and severally on an unsecured subordinated basis: Apollo Asset Management, Apollo Principal Holdings A, B and C, AMH Holdings (Delaware), and Apollo Management Holdings.
Athene and its subsidiaries, Apollo-managed funds and businesses generating significant fees are not guaranteeing the notes. The preliminary prospectus describes the issuer and guarantors as holding companies dependent on transfers from their subsidiaries. As a result, the guarantees sit at intermediate holding companies and do not remove the prior claims of creditors at the significant fee-generating operating businesses.
As of September 30, 2026, the issuer and guarantors had $4.684 billion of senior indebtedness and $1.078 billion of indebtedness ranking on a parity with the notes. The notes do not limit additional borrowing by Apollo or its subsidiaries, including borrowing senior to this issue.
The expected ratings are A3 from Moody’s and BBB+ from both S&P and Fitch. Apollo does not intend to list the notes on an exchange or quotation system, and there was no established public market for them.
Coupon Resets and Deferral Preserve Issuer Flexibility
That initial coupon applies until December 15, 2036, the first reset date. For each subsequent reset period, the rate will equal the five-year U.S. Treasury rate as of the most recent reset determination date plus 2.672%. Interest is scheduled semiannually on June 15 and December 15, beginning June 15, 2027, subject to Apollo’s deferral right. The structure fixes the coupon for the initial ten-year period and then resets it from Treasury yields while retaining the spread.
Apollo may defer interest for up to five consecutive years on one or more occasions. Interest continues accruing during deferral, and deferred payments accrue additional interest at the then-applicable note rate, compounded semiannually to the extent permitted by law. During a deferral period, Apollo and the guarantors generally face restrictions on payments on, or redemptions and purchases of, their equity and parity or junior debt, subject to enumerated exceptions. Deferral therefore postpones cash payments rather than canceling the interest obligation.
Apollo may redeem some or all of the notes at 100% of principal plus accrued and unpaid interest during the three months before and including the first reset date or any later reset date. Separate rights permit whole-issue redemption within 120 days of a tax redemption event at the same price or a rating agency event at 102% of principal, in each case plus accrued and unpaid interest. Holders do not have an option to require redemption before maturity.
Mubadala Transaction Provides the Named Use of Proceeds
The October 26, 2026 transaction announcement said Apollo will take a minority equity stake in Mubadala Capital and commit capital across its investment strategies. Additional strategic investors will also join as minority shareholders. Apollo and those investors are expected to commit an aggregate $5 billion to Mubadala Capital’s strategies at initial close, a combined amount rather than an Apollo-only commitment.
Mubadala Investment Company will remain the majority shareholder, while Mubadala Capital will continue to operate independently with its own governance structure and its existing management retaining full authority over investment decisions and operations.
Mubadala Capital reported that its core alternatives business managed and invested more than $60 billion across five strategies. The October announcement targeted a fourth-quarter 2026 closing, subject to regulatory and legal approvals.
The offering pairs long-dated funding and a named strategic use with considerable issuer flexibility through reset-date redemptions and interest deferral. The offset is in the creditor claim: repayment ranks behind senior debt and non-guarantor subsidiary liabilities, while the six guarantees come from holding companies rather than Athene or the businesses generating significant fees.

Path Robotics raises $300M at $2.45B valuation to scale physical AI for manufacturing
Annual recurring revenue grew 17-fold over 18 months as the Columbus startup added industrial deployments. Customers include HII, Lockheed Martin and Saronic, while a $600 million performance-based shipbuilding agreement and plans to reach 400 employees by year-end underscore its growth.
Ohio Tech News
10 Nov 2026
— 3 min read
Share
Path Robotics co-founders and brothers Andy and Alex Lonsberry (Photo: Path Robotics)
Columbus-based Path Robotics has raised $300 million in Series E financing at a $2.45 billion post-money valuation to expand its robotic welding business and bring its artificial intelligence technology to more manufacturing tasks.
AI-focused growth equity firm Georgian led the round, announced Nov. 10, with participation from existing investors including Drive Capital. The financing brings Path’s total funding to more than $610 million since its founding in 2018, according to the company. Georgian partner Emily Walsh will join its board of directors.
The investment follows rapid commercial growth. Path said annual recurring revenue increased 17-fold over the past 18 months as it expanded deployments among industrial customers across North America.
The new capital will support additional deployments, development of new robotic platforms, and increased investment in computing resources and AI model training. In a LinkedIn post , CEO and co-founder Andy Lonsberry said Path plans to begin expanding its technology beyond welding into other production-line tasks in 2027.
“Our goal isn't to automate one step, but to automate the entire factory,” Lonsberry said in the announcement.
Scaling across shipbuilding and heavy industry
Path’s expansion targets a production challenge: manufacturers with demand for more products but limited capacity to build them.
The company develops physical AI—technology that enables robots to perceive their surroundings and adapt their actions to changing conditions. Its initial focus has been welding, where variations in parts and joints can make conventional, preprogrammed automation difficult to deploy.
Path said its customers include HII, Lockheed Martin and Saronic, along with manufacturers such as EK Machine, Millerbernd Manufacturing Company, TransAmerican Power Products and TYCROP. Its target industries include shipbuilding and defense, heavy equipment, and energy infrastructure.
Earlier this year, Path announced a $600 million performance-based production agreement with HII to accelerate deployment of its technology across U.S. Navy shipbuilding programs. That agreement is separate from the equity financing announced Nov. 10.
To support growing demand, Path said its workforce has increased 97% year over year, with plans to reach 400 employees by the end of 2026.
Taking its AI beyond welding
At the center of Path’s technology is Obsidian, a physical AI welding model that uses real-world production data to help robots identify weld joints, plan and execute welds, and adapt to changing conditions, according to the company.
Path recently introduced Rove, a mobile welding system that pairs Obsidian with a four-legged robot. The system is designed to bring welding capabilities directly to a part rather than requiring the work to take place inside a stationary robotic cell.
The funding will help Path extend its technology to additional robotic platforms and manufacturing applications.
Walsh said Path’s growing base of production data could help strengthen its technology as deployments expand, “The team has built a strong foundation in welding, and we see enormous potential for Path Robotics to extend that intelligence to new manufacturing applications and industries."
Other participants in the financing included existing investors Addition, IronArc Ventures, Tiger Global, and Yamaha Motor Ventures and its affiliates, along with D. E. Shaw Ventures and NAVER Ventures.
From an Ohio garage to the factory floor
For Lonsberry, the production problem has roots in his family’s Ohio manufacturing experience.
In his LinkedIn post, he said he learned to weld at age 8 in the family garage. His father later turned that garage into a manufacturing company in Warren, where Lonsberry saw firsthand the challenges of building a U.S. manufacturing business.
Before starting Path, Lonsberry said he and fellow co-founder and brother Alex Lonsberry spoke with more than 100 U.S. manufacturers. They repeatedly heard the same concern: backlogs were growing, but production was not.
“The challenge wasn't product demand. It was production,” he wrote.

candidates.text:
DefenseTech
Palantir Alumni’s Onodrim Raises $300 Million to Buy Up Europe’s Defense Suppliers
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 09. November 2026, 09:06
Onodrim Industries raised $300 million in a Series A round. © Fred Hayes / Getty Images for Onodrim Industries
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Europe has a new defense unicorn, and it doesn’t build a single drone itself: Onodrim Industries, based in Amsterdam, has closed a $300 million Series A round. The company is now valued at $1.3 billion. Founded by former Palantir employees, it plans to use the money to take majority stakes in established suppliers to the defense, aerospace and manufacturing industries.
The Year’s Largest Series A
The round was led by Lux Capital, an early backer of Anduril, according to the company’s press release . New and existing investors including General Catalyst, Lakestar, Altimeter, Strike Capital, 137 Ventures, 8090 and Expeditions also took part. Onodrim says it is the largest European Series A of 2026. The company raised more than $45 million earlier this year.
The round ended up considerably larger than first planned. In late September, Bloomberg reported that Onodrim was seeking about 200 million euros at a $1 billion valuation.
Buy, Digitize, Scale
The business model looks more like private equity than a typical start-up. Onodrim plans to invest in manufacturers whose products have both civilian and military uses and that sit in the defense industry’s supply chains, where bottlenecks are currently common. The acquired companies are to receive long-term capital along with software and Onodrim’s own engineering teams, who will digitize production and develop new products so the companies can take on larger defense contracts.
Europe has many outstanding companies, but they often lack the resources to grow as fast as is now needed, said Aistis Šimaitis, Onodrim’s co-founder and chief executive. The company plans to announce its first acquisitions in the coming months. Its co-founder Alex Blessing is directly inviting owners of defense, aerospace and industrial businesses to get in touch.
Palantir DNA and an Office in Munich
Mr. Šimaitis previously advised the Lithuanian government, held a senior technology role at Palantir Technologies and earned a doctorate at the University of Oxford. Alexander Blessing, the chief technology officer, studied at Stanford and Cambridge and worked at Palantir as a forward deployed engineer, embedded directly with customers. The founding team also includes Christian Garrett, a partner at 137 Ventures. In addition to Amsterdam, London and Vilnius, Onodrim is now opening offices in Munich and Turin.
Investors are betting on the model. Europe needs a stronger industrial foundation to meet the security challenges ahead, said Brandon Reeves, a partner at Lux Capital. Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, president of General Catalyst, sees Onodrim as redefining the industrial conglomerate: Europe’s established manufacturers already have the expertise, customers and trust, she said, but they lack cutting-edge technology.
The Competition
Onodrim is entering a booming market. European defense tech companies are raising billions, led by Munich-based Helsing, which recently raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation , and Quantum Systems. Buying established manufacturers is not a new recipe either: Helsing has already acquired the Bavarian aircraft maker Grob Aircraft . But while most start-ups develop their own software, drones or systems, Onodrim is betting entirely on acquisitions in a fragmented supplier market where lead times are often measured in years.
Winning the Trust of Defense Ministries
Whether the bet pays off remains to be seen. According to The Financial Times, the open questions are whether venture capital can consolidate the supplier base quickly enough and whether defense ministries will trust a company founded only about a year ago. Defense contracts have historically gone to the large established prime contractors. On top of that, Onodrim has yet to complete a single acquisition. Its $1.3 billion valuation therefore rests mainly on its team, its investors and its promise to buy quickly in a capital-hungry market.

Swiss VC Redalpine Raises $250 Million for A.I., Robotics and Biotech
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 10. November 2026, 08:00
The redalpine team, which has closed its eighth early-stage fund at $250 million. © redalpine
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
While many venture capital firms spend months courting investors, Redalpine was done in less than a year: The Swiss firm has closed its eighth early-stage fund, Redalpine Capital VIII (RAC VIII), at $250 million. The fund was oversubscribed and is larger than its predecessor, which closed at $200 million in 2024. Redalpine now manages more than $1.4 billion in total.
Where the Money Is Going
With RAC VIII, Redalpine plans to invest in about 20 European start-ups at the seed to Series A stage, selected from more than 5,000 companies it reviews each year. Checks range from $1 million to $15 million, and Redalpine often leads the rounds. The focus is on companies at the intersection of software and science. Half of the investment team has a background in the natural sciences or engineering, according to Redalpine.
The first three investments from the new fund:
Enact Intelligence: The Zurich robotics start-up aims to give robots a sense of touch and recently raised a $30 million pre-seed round with backing from Yann LeCun, among others.
Helical: The London start-up is building a virtual A.I. lab for drug discovery. Redalpine previously led its $10 million seed round .
Arlequin AI: The team, based in Paris, Berlin and London, is developing an A.I. architecture to protect critical systems and works with government agencies.
Sebastian Becker, a general partner, said artificial intelligence was leveling the playing field for founders around the world, giving the edge to those who best understand the science behind a product and the hardest problems.
Aviva, Flexstone and KfW as Backers
The limited partners in RAC VIII include existing and new investors, among them the British asset manager Aviva Investors, Flexstone Partners and the German development bank KfW. Redalpine was founded in Zurich in 2006, is now based in Zug and has offices in Berlin and London.
Its portfolio includes well-known names such as Mistral AI, N26 and Proxima Fusion. Redalpine led the Munich fusion start-up’s seed round, and in the summer, Proxima raised €411 million at a €2.4 billion valuation . Since 2023, Redalpine says it has sold or taken public 12 portfolio companies. They include the Swiss biotech Araris, which the Japanese drugmaker Taiho acquired for up to $1.14 billion , and, according to Redalpine, Memo Therapeutics (to Ipsen) and the A.I. security start-up Lakera (to Check Point). Companies from its previous fund, RAC VII, have raised more than $1.1 billion from investors in total.
The Competition
Redalpine is not the only firm raising fresh capital for European tech start-ups this year. In Zurich, Lakestar closed Lakestar Resilience I, a $300 million fund for defense and dual-use technologies. Headline raised $400 million for its eighth fund, which targets seed and Series A rounds in A.I., and Accel’s new European fund comes to $800 million. In Germany, Uplift Ventures launched a €100 million deep-tech fund that also invests in seed to Series A rounds.
Money Flows to Established Players
Fund-raising remains difficult for many venture firms, however. European venture funds raised $14.9 billion across 111 funds through the end of September 2026, compared with $15.5 billion in all of last year, according to PitchBook data compiled by SeedBlink . The money is concentrating in the largest funds, and the market beyond them remains tight, according to PitchBook. In the DACH region, 83 venture funds closed with a combined €6.2 billion in 2022, while in the first nine months of 2025, only 21 funds closed with €2.0 billion, according to PitchBook. The median time from launch to final close is 26 months.
That favors established firms with a record of exits, such as Redalpine, while new and smaller fund managers face a tougher climb. Deep-tech start-ups also often need many years and a lot of capital before they generate revenue or can be sold. Whether the bets on fusion energy, robotics and A.I.-driven biotech pay off will therefore only become clear many years from now.

Modern Wealth Management has secured a $200 million hybrid debt-and-equity investment from funds managed by Centerbridge Partners to support additional acquisitions and expansion of its national wealth management platform. Modern Wealth will also remain majority employee-owned.
The company currently has more than 150 employee shareholders.

The firm has grown through a combination of acquisitions and organic expansion.
Its operating model focuses on integrating established financial advisory businesses into a platform providing centralized technology, operations, and specialized planning services.
Modern Wealth serves clients through investment management, financial planning, tax planning and preparation, estate planning, and other wealth management capabilities.
The company believes these services allow advisors to address increasingly complex financial needs while maintaining relationships with their clients.
Its acquisition strategy emphasizes partnerships with independent advisory firms seeking additional operational resources and opportunities for long-term growth.
Acquired businesses gain access to the firm’s technology, investment expertise, and centralized support infrastructure.

Management believes that centralizing certain activities can allow advisors to devote more time to client service and organic growth.

During that period, Modern Wealth has completed 26 acquisitions and expanded its assets under management to nearly $17 billion.
The company’s growth reflects an ongoing trend within the registered investment advisory industry toward consolidation and the development of larger independent wealth management platforms.

Crestview manages funds with more than $10 billion in aggregate capital commitments and has supported Modern Wealth since its launch.

candidates.title: Modular Data Center Startup Mavria Raises $130M, but Grid Hookups Remain Unproven
candidates.snippet: Modular Data Center Startup Mavria Raises $130M, but Grid Hookups Remain Unproven Tech Times
candidates.text:
By
Shannon Harwood
Published: Nov 10 2026, 2:10 AM EST
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp
Mavria
Mavria, a data center startup whose founders include former Energy Department officials, announced Monday that it raised $130 million at a $1 billion valuation to build data centers in a factory. The company was founded in June 2026 , according to co-founder Seth Cohen, and its first unit, Terrain 01, is being built in Houston .
Terrain comes in 5 MW units, according to Dealroom , which cites the Wall Street Journal's reporting. Mavria's own announcement gives no capacity figure , and the company has not named customers or published capacity, pricing or delivery timelines.
For the frontier AI labs, cloud providers and data center developers that Mavria targets, the open question is power, not factory speed. DatacenterDynamics reported that Mavria says Terrain can bypass grid delays by plugging into local distribution lines to soak up excess capacity, but the company's announcement makes no grid connection claim . That makes size the number to watch in Texas, where Senate Bill 6 covers loads of at least 75 megawatts at a single site: one 5 MW block is about 7% of that line, while a 100 MW campus would need 20 blocks.
How Terrain Packs Power, Cooling and Compute Into One 5 MW Block
Mavria says Terrain replaces on-site custom construction with factory-based repeatable manufacturing . Customers' compute runs inside it, and the company says it supplies infrastructure without operating a cloud or selling compute .
HuggingNews reports that the units use direct liquid cooling and integrated power distribution for customer-owned compute. Mavria's announcement mentions neither the liquid cooling nor the block size.
Liquid cooling matters at this size because AI racks outrun air. Wikipedia's computer-cooling entry puts air cooling up to 23 kW per rack, while NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack draws 190 to 230 kW , according to earlier TechTimes reporting. At those figures, 5 MW supports roughly 22 to 26 such racks before cooling and power-conversion overhead, and Mavria has not said which hardware Terrain targets.
Factory integration removes on-site assembly work, not the utility connection. NVIDIA's DSX POD moves cabling, power distribution and cooling piping into a factory, shortening connection time from roughly six months to 14 days , yet the pod still arrives at a prepared site that must already have high-voltage power , a coolant loop and a network handoff. Dealroom likewise notes that factory production cannot by itself solve power availability or site-connection delays.
The tradeoff is standardization. Mavria says Terrain should bring more predictable delivery and lower costs , but it has published no pricing , so the benefit remains a claim.
Related
NVIDIA Cuts AI Factory Deployment to 14 Days With DSX POD at GTC Berlin
FluidStack Closes $1.5B: Revenue Soars From $1.8M to $660M Projected While Owning Zero Chips
Can Factory-Built Data Centers Really Use Spare Local Power Capacity?
Distribution networks step transmission voltage down to primary lines of 4 to 35 kilovolts , with 12.47, 25 and 34.5 kV common in the United States. The utility-consulting firm Logic20/20 says smaller enterprise and colocation sites typically under 20 megawatts connect at the distribution level, a band that includes a 5 MW block.
Spare capacity on a feeder is finite, and high ambient temperatures limit the power ratings of transformers, cables and lines. Mavria's announcement names no utility , connection voltage or energization schedule for a Terrain block.
The market backdrop is real but disputed. Sightline Climate estimated in February that 30% to 50% of large data centers due online in 2026 would be delayed, citing power constraints, equipment shortages and local opposition, with about 5 GW under construction against at least 16 GW planned. Axios noted that most affected projects were delayed rather than canceled, with nine canceled projects tracked. SemiAnalysis argued in June that the headline claim rests on a flawed denominator and on speculative early-stage announcements.
Texas's 75 MW Large-Load Line and Abbott's Audit Pause Make Block Count Decisive
Senate Bill 6, signed June 20, 2025, directs the PUCT to create interconnection procedures for large loads, and its definition allows the PUCT to lower the 75 MW threshold. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) standards are to include a transmission screening study fee of no less than $100,000 for covered loads, and the commission voted March 12 to publish a draft rule implementing them.
On Aug. 3, Gov. Greg Abbott directed a comprehensive audit of data center projects advancing through the interconnection process run by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which Foley says effectively pauses approvals. ERCOT is tracking more than 1,800 large-load projects totaling over 474 GW of potential demand, about 90% of it for data centers, though many are preliminary and may never be built.
Block count still matters. A campus of 15 or more blocks would reach the statutory 75 MW line, and the PUCT can lower it. Abbott's directive applies to data centers in the ERCOT queue regardless of load size , while purely behind-the-meter, on-site-generation projects that do not interconnect through ERCOT may not be subject to it. The legal summaries reviewed do not say whether a small site on a utility's distribution line would enter the ERCOT queue and fall under the audit, and Mavria has not said where customers will place Terrain.
Politics add uncertainty. Of 45 data center ballot measures tracked across 10 states, 33 had passed by the morning after the Nov. 3 election, according to Data Centers on the Ballot.

candidates.text:
Carsten Hoefer
dpa
(TNS)
Munich — German start-up Vaeridion has raised over €120 million ($135 million) in funding from the European Union and investors to develop an electric aircraft, the Munich-based company said on Thursday.
Vaeridion said it had raised €30 million from venture capital investors in its latest funding round. The European Commission had previously made €94.5 million available from its Innovation Fund.
The company is developing a nine-seat passenger aircraft for regional air travel called the Microliner. Vaeridion says it has already received purchase commitments for 130 aircraft.
With the €30 million from investors, Vaeridion wants to build a prototype that is eligible for certification. The EU money is intended for final assembly and for setting up production at the German aviation research and development centre at Oberpfaffenhofen airport. The hub is home to a large branch of the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), and several companies have set up operations nearby.
Vaeridion is aiming to provide a cheaper alternative to the more than 21,000 small, ageing turboprop aircraft that fly on regional routes worldwide. The company's electric aircraft is designed to have a range of 400 kilometres and operate without kerosene.
According to the start-up's calculations, Microliner tickets should cost roughly the same as first-class tickets on Germany's high-speed rail network.
"Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide," said chief executive Ivor von Dartel, a former Airbus manager.
The company says its first customer is the ASL Group, a business aviation operator in Belgium and the Netherlands.
Past failures
Two German electric plane start-ups have already failed. The Munich-based company Lilium went insolvent twice before giving up for good.
A second company, Volocopter, also went insolvent and was subsequently sold to Chinese investors.
Other companies are also working on electric aircraft, including the Bavarian start-up ERC System, which is developing a plane with a hybrid engine for transporting patients and other purposes.

Made to Order gives organizations a different route to access new technology. Rather than buying an existing company and adapting it, a client defines the exact capability it needs. XLIO then funds and builds a dedicated startup to deliver it, located and incorporated wherever best suits the client. Once the company hits agreed KPIs, usually within one to three years, the client acquires both team and technology. Deals typically range from $10 million to $50 million.

"Austin's startup economy is vibrant," said Ron Kornfeld, CEO of XLIO Ventures. Yoco Technologies , the South African fintech company backed by global private equity firm TPG Inc., has secured a $100 million credit facility from Victory Park Capital Advisors LLC (VPC), a U.S.-based alternative investment manager with approximately $3.6 billion in assets under management.
The funding represents a significant milestone for Yoco as it continues expanding its financial services ecosystem for small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) across South Africa.
Funding to Expand Merchant Financing
According to reports, Yoco plans to use the new credit facility to strengthen and expand financing opportunities available to its growing network of merchants.
The company has evolved beyond its origins as a point-of-sale (POS) payments provider and now offers a broader suite of digital commerce solutions designed to help small businesses accept payments, manage operations, and access working capital.
The $100 million facility will enable Yoco to extend additional funding to merchants that use its platform, helping business owners access capital needed to purchase inventory, invest in growth, manage cash flow, or navigate seasonal fluctuations.
Access to affordable financing remains one of the biggest challenges facing SMEs in South Africa, making merchant-lending solutions an increasingly important area of growth for fintech companies.
Yoco’s Evolution Into a Full-Service Fintech Platform
Founded in 2015, Yoco initially built its reputation by providing simple card payment devices and digital payment solutions to small businesses that were often underserved by traditional banks.
Over time, the company expanded its offering to include:
Payment acceptance solutions
Point-of-sale systems
Business management tools
Online payment services
Merchant cash advances and financing products
Digital commerce solutions
Today, Yoco serves hundreds of thousands of merchants across South Africa, ranging from informal traders and restaurants to retail stores and service-based businesses.
The company’s technology-driven approach enables it to analyse transaction histories and business performance data, allowing it to offer financing products tailored to merchants’ actual business activity rather than relying solely on traditional credit assessments.
Strategic Backing From TPG
Yoco has attracted significant investor interest in recent years, including backing from TPG Inc. , one of the world’s largest private equity and alternative asset management firms. The involvement of TPG has provided Yoco with additional capital and strategic support as it expands its footprint within South Africa’s rapidly growing digital payments market.
The latest facility from Victory Park Capital further strengthens Yoco’s ability to scale its lending operations without diluting existing shareholders, as debt financing allows the company to access growth capital while maintaining ownership structures.
Victory Park Capital’s Growing Fintech Portfolio
Victory Park Capital has become an active investor in financial technology and alternative lending businesses globally.
The firm specializes in providing flexible capital solutions to companies operating in sectors such as:
Financial services
Fintech
Consumer lending
Asset-backed finance
Small business financing
Its financing structures are often designed to help high-growth companies scale lending activities and reach underserved customer segments. The partnership with Yoco aligns with VPC’s broader strategy of supporting technology-enabled financial services platforms that increase financial inclusion and improve access to capital.
Boosting Financial Inclusion for South African SMEs
The new funding arrives at a time when digital financial services are playing an increasingly important role in South Africa’s small-business sector. Many entrepreneurs continue to face difficulties accessing traditional bank financing due to limited collateral, insufficient credit history, or lengthy approval processes.
By leveraging merchant transaction data and digital payment records, fintech companies such as Yoco are helping to bridge this gap and provide businesses with faster, more accessible funding options. The $100 million facility is expected to strengthen Yoco’s ability to meet growing demand for working-capital solutions among its merchant base while supporting broader efforts to improve financial inclusion for South Africa’s SME sector.
Outlook
The agreement with Victory Park Capital marks another major step in Yoco’s transformation from a payments provider into a comprehensive financial platform for small businesses. With access to $100 million in additional capital, the company is well positioned to expand its merchant financing operations, deepen customer relationships, and support the growth of thousands of South African businesses.
As fintech-driven lending continues to gain momentum across Africa, Yoco’s latest funding deal underscores investor confidence in digital financial services and the critical role they play in helping small businesses access the capital needed to grow and thrive.

NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / November 10, 2026 / Daylight, which combines AI agents with human security experts to detect, investigate, and respond to cyber threats, today announced an $80 million Series B led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, with existing investors Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital. The round brings Daylight's total funding to $120 million. Daylight's revenue has surged more than 40x over the past year, fueled by rapidly growing demand from Fortune 500 enterprises and leading AI-native companies. Its customer base includes Lovable, LastPass, Rogo, dLocal, and Miro.
October's wave of cyber incidents, dubbed "Black October," stretched incident response teams already under pressure from increasingly complex security threats. As organizations turn to AI to help manage these mounting demands, the technology isn't necessarily easing the burden. A July 2026 ISC2 survey found that 65% of cybersecurity professionals using AI now spend more time determining whether to trust its recommendations than they did a year ago, while 63% spend more time verifying its outputs.
The challenge goes beyond AI adoption. Companies also struggle to find security services that fit their specific needs. Traditional managed security providers offer rigid, one-size-fits-all services, while standalone AI tools often leave companies managing yet another system. Some organizations want to outsource security operations entirely, while others have internal teams and want to retain control over their detections and processes. As a result, enterprises are left piecing together multiple vendors for detection and response, threat hunting, phishing, data protection, and security data management.
Daylight brings these capabilities together through a flexible service model that combines AI automation with some of the world's top security engineering talent, expertise that most companies struggle to recruit and retain. Its AI-native platform and security engineers continuously build, run, and customize AI agents to each customer's systems, workflows, risks, and priorities. The agents handle day-to-day security operations, while engineers focus on decisions requiring human judgment. Customers can choose how the service is delivered, whether fully managed, co-managed alongside their internal teams, or supported by forward-deployed engineers.

Those detections run through Daylight's full MDR workflow, where AI activity is investigated alongside identity, endpoint, cloud, SaaS, and business context. The capability is already in use by enterprise customers, including Miro.
"The future of security operations won't be defined by how many people a company can deploy, but by how effectively AI agents can take on increasingly complex security work," said Hagai Shapira, co-founder and CEO of Daylight . "As these agents become more capable, they'll fundamentally change how threats are detected, investigated, and contained, with expert security engineers implementing, governing, and continuously improving their operations. At Daylight, we're already bringing this vision to life through an agent-native model that combines the speed and scale of AI with the judgment and oversight of human experts. We're building the foundation for a new era of security operations."
"Cybersecurity remains a top priority for enterprises of all sizes, and we see a significant opportunity for agentic technologies to transform how security outcomes are delivered," said Irit Kahan, Managing Director and Global Head of Cyber Security Investing within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. "By scaling human expertise with agentic technology, Daylight has the potential to enable organizations to respond at machine speed, with greater accuracy and at scale."
George Foster, Investor within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives added, "Daylight continues to drive innovation in this space, scaling high-level security expertise through the use of agentic technology. We believe this combination positions the company to have the potential to become a leader in the next-generation of cybersecurity."
Daylight was founded by Hagai Shapira and Eldad Rudich, who first met while serving in an elite Israeli military intelligence unit. Shapira was an early product leader at cybersecurity unicorn Torq, where he worked closely with enterprise security teams, while Rudich was Torq's first employee and VP of R&D, building its core platform and engineering organization from the ground up.
